newsitem.title: UK: New opportunites will soothe EMU, hit bonds - Salomon.
newsitem.headline: New opportunites will soothe EMU, hit bonds - Salomon.

text.p: The number of bond derivatives traded after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) will shrink but new trading opportunities will arise, Salomon Brothers' chief executive said on Thursday.
"EMU will add to competitive pressures in the industry by merging several markets into one big euro market," Salomon's Peter Middleton told a conference on EMU in London.

He said the number of interest rate contracts would likely slim by half from around 16 when EMU begins in 1999. If Spain and Italy were included in EMU, the number of contracts would fall further to three, he said.
The number bond contracts would be cut to around nine from 27 and to five if Spain and Italy are in, Middleton said.

Middleton said he expected trade to focus on German and France as benchmarks but added that he was not sure if one benchmark bond would have a big enough pool of deliverable contracts to support trade.
This could lead to squeezes and reduced liquidity. One solution would be to have multi-country contracts deliverable into the same bond, he said.
Although the number of contracts would shrink after EMU the volume of turnover would not necessarily drop, Middleton said.
"Clearly somebody who trades the French/German spread has got to find something else to do. But any job losses will be offset by new opportunities," he said.
Middleton noted that turnover in U.S. T-bond futures roughly matches the total turnover of bond contracts of the countries destined for EMU.
Eurodollar contract turnover is significantly higher than the interest rate futures of potential EMU countries combined, including Spain and Italy, he said.
Middleton said that although EMU eliminates currency risk, it also eliminates an individual country's ability to print money. Bond markets, therefore, would put greater emphasis on credit risk.
"This implies a fundamental change in the risks of the holders of these country bonds. Government debt no longer provides a riskless benchmark," he said.
"Credit risk will become the main determinant in spreads between government bonds."
Credit risk will also be important for companies, Middleton said. Companies with heavy exposure to countries like Italy, for example, will have a much greater desire to hedge their credit risks.
This will lead to a high demand for derivaties on credit risks like options on credit spreads.
